citations.quote:
Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

The map
$$\Phi:\mathbb C\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad \Phi(a+bi)=(a,b),$$
is a bijection. Under it,
$$\Phi((a+bi)+(u+vi))=(a+u,b+v)$$
and
$$\Phi((a+bi)(u+vi))=(au-bv,av+bu).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: [Coordinate expressions] Fix $(x,t)\in\Omega\times I$ and write $\psi=\psi(x,t)$. Since $\overline{\psi}=u-iv$ and $\partial_x\psi=\partial_xu+i\,\partial_xv$, [F1] gives $\overline{\psi}\,\partial_x\psi=(u\,\partial_xu+v\,\partial_xv)+i\,(u\,\partial_xv-(\partial_xu)\,v)$, hence $\operatorname{Im}(\overline{\psi}\,\partial_x\psi)=u\,\partial_xv-(\partial_xu)\,v$ and $|\psi|^2=u^2+v^2$; the two displays of the statement for $n$ and $j$ therefore agree at every point.

[Differentiating the density] By [F2] applied pointwise, $\partial_tn=2u\,\partial_tu+2v\,\partial_tv$. Substituting the two given equations, written as $\partial_tu=\hbar^{-1}\bigl(Vv-\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2v\bigr)$ and $\partial_tv=\hbar^{-1}\bigl(\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\partial_x^2u-Vu\bigr)$, gives $\partial_tn=\frac{2}{\hbar}\bigl(uVv-\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}u\,\partial_x^2v+\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}v\,\partial_x^2u-vVu\bigr)=\frac{\hbar}{m}\bigl(v\,\partial_x^2u-u\,\partial_x^2v\bigr)$, because $2\hbar^{-1}\cdot\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}=\tfrac{\hbar}{m}$ and the two terms containing $Vuv$ cancel.

[Stationary flux has zero derivative] In the situation of (b), [F2] gives $j_{\mathrm s}'(x)=\frac{\hbar}{m}\bigl(u_{\mathrm s}'(x)v_{\mathrm s}'(x)+u_{\mathrm s}(x)v_{\mathrm s}''(x)-u_{\mathrm s}''(x)v_{\mathrm s}(x)-u_{\mathrm s}'(x)v_{\mathrm s}'(x)\bigr)=\frac{\hbar}{m}\bigl(u_{\mathrm s}(x)v_{\mathrm s}''(x)-u_{\mathrm s}''(x)v_{\mathrm s}(x)\bigr)$ at every $x\in\Omega$. The two stationary equations give $u_{\mathrm s}''=\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}(V-E)u_{\mathrm s}$ and $v_{\mathrm s}''=\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}(V-E)v_{\mathrm s}$ pointwise, so $j_{\mathrm s}'=\frac{\hbar}{m}\cdot\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}(V-E)(u_{\mathrm s}v_{\mathrm s}-u_{\mathrm s}v_{\mathrm s})=0$ on $\Omega$.

[Differentiating the flux] By [F2] applied pointwise, $\partial_xj=\frac{\hbar}{m}\bigl(\partial_xu\,\partial_xv+u\,\partial_x^2v-\partial_x^2u\,v-\partial_xu\,\partial_xv\bigr)=\frac{\hbar}{m}\bigl(u\,\partial_x^2v-(\partial_x^2u)\,v\bigr)$. Adding the result of step 1.2 gives $\partial_tn+\partial_xj=\frac{\hbar}{m}\bigl(v\,\partial_x^2u-u\,\partial_x^2v+u\,\partial_x^2v-v\,\partial_x^2u\bigr)=0$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, which is (a).

[Constancy] The functions $u_{\mathrm s},v_{\mathrm s},u_{\mathrm s}',v_{\mathrm s}'$ are continuous on the open interval $\Omega$ by hypothesis, so $j_{\mathrm s}=\frac{\hbar}{m}(u_{\mathrm s}v_{\mathrm s}'-u_{\mathrm s}'v_{\mathrm s})$ is continuous on $\Omega$ by [F3], and $\Omega$ is order-convex; with $j_{\mathrm s}'=0$ at every point of $\Omega$ by step 1.3, [F4] makes $j_{\mathrm s}$ constant on $\Omega$. This proves (b), and step 2.1 proved (a).

boundaries.evidence: The intervals $\Omega$ and $I$ are nonempty by hypothesis; step 1.1 evaluates the identity at every given point and no empty index set or empty domain occurs.
Step 1.1 includes the identically zero $\psi$, for which $n$ and $j$ vanish; step 1.2 and step 3.1 then give $j=0$ without dividing by any quantity.
The lemma is scalar-valued and one-dimensional: step 1.1 uses one complex function and its two real parts, and step 3.1 one constant.
The identities of step 1.2 and step 2.1 hold for arbitrary real functions, including proportional or coincident parts; no independence of $u$ and $v$ is assumed.
The identity and the constancy are proved on the open intervals $\Omega$ and $I$, exactly as the statement requires; step 3.1 uses no endpoint value, and no boundary condition is asserted.
The statement assumes Countable Choice as the hypothesis of the cited supplier, and steps 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 make no selection of any kind.

boundaries.reason: Part (a) is a pointwise identity and part (b) a one-directional constancy conclusion; the lemma contains no if-and-only-if pair whose forward direction could require a separate check.
No converse is claimed: the lemma never asserts that a constant current forces the stationary equation, so there is no reverse implication to discharge.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice and let $n\ge1$. For every $u\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ and every multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$,
$$\mathcal F(D^\alpha u)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal Fu\qquad\text{in }\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n),$$
where $D^\alpha$ is the distributional derivative of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]] and $\mathcal F$ is
the negative-sign $2\pi$-normalized transform. Moreover, if $u=u_f$ and
$D^\alpha u=u_g$ for $L^2$ classes $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb R^n)$ and their regular
distributions, then the unitary Plancherel transforms satisfy
$$\mathcal F_2g(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\mathcal F_2f(\xi)\qquad\text{for almost every }\xi\in\mathbb R^n.$$
The second assertion compares the Plancherel classes only; it neither asserts
pointwise values of arbitrary representatives nor presupposes any Sobolev-space
notation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

derivations.claim: [Domain] By [F2] the sets $D(H_0)$ and $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ coincide, and by [F1] a class $u\in L^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ has a second weak derivative in $L^2$ exactly when $\xi\mapsto(2\pi\xi)^2\mathcal F_2u(\xi)$ is in $L^2$, i.e. exactly when $|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2u\in L^2$; this is the defining condition of $D(H_0)$ in the statement, so the domain identity of (a) holds with no appeal to any additional regularity.

[Multiplier comparison] Fix $f\in D(H_0)$. By [F2], $\mathcal F_2(H_0f)(\xi)=c|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f(\xi)$ for almost every $\xi$. Let $g:=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\,D^2f$; since $f\in W^{2,2}$, $D^2f\in L^2$ and [F1] gives $\mathcal F_2g(\xi)=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\bigl(-4\pi^2\xi^2\bigr)\mathcal F_2f(\xi)=\frac{2\pi^2\hbar^2}{m}\xi^2\mathcal F_2f(\xi)=c|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f(\xi)$ for almost every $\xi$. Hence $\mathcal F_2(H_0f-g)=0$ in $L^2$, and [F3] gives $H_0f=g$. This proves (a).

[Bounded perturbations] Let $V$ be real, bounded and measurable and let $f\in D(H_0)$. By step 1.1 $f\in W^{2,2}$, so $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}D^2f\in L^2$ by [F1] and $Vf\in L^2$ because $V$ is bounded; moreover $(H_0+M_V)f=H_0f+Vf=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}D^2f+Vf$ by step 1.2 and the definition of $M_V$, on the common domain $D(H_0)=D(M_V)\cap D(H_0)$ of clause (c) of the cited theorem. Since the two operators have the same domain and the same values, they coincide; the eigenvalue equation and the weak equation are therefore the same elementwise identity in $L^2$. This proves (b).

boundaries.evidence: The statement fixes dimension one and the domain $\mathbb R$, which is nonempty; step 1.1 identifies the two domains and uses no empty family.
Step 1.2 includes the zero class, for which both operators vanish; step 2.1 includes the free case $V=0$ as the degenerate bounded perturbation.
The one-dimensional case $d=1$ is the stated setting, and step 1.1 uses the single multiplier $-4\pi^2\xi^2$ with no component index.
Step 1.2 compares multipliers almost everywhere and step 2.1 treats an arbitrary bounded measurable $V$, with no independence or nondegeneracy hypothesis.
The operators act on classes on all of $\mathbb R$; step 1.1 uses only the almost-everywhere Plancherel transforms and no endpoint behaviour.
The statement assumes Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice through the operator theorem, and steps 1.2 and 2.1 make no selection.

boundaries.reason: The lemma states identities between operators and domains; it contains no if-and-only-if clause whose forward direction could be checked separately.
No converse is asserted: the lemma does not claim that any other operator has multiplier $c|\xi|^2$ or domain equal to $W^{2,2}$.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $T$ be a
densely defined linear operator on $H$, with domain $D(T)$ dense in $H$
([[def-densely-defined-closed-and-closable-operator]], [[def-dense-top]]).
Since $D(T)$ is dense, and since $H$ is complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]), every
bounded linear functional on the normed space $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]) extends uniquely to a bounded linear
functional $\widetilde\varphi$ on $H$ of the same norm, by setting
$\widetilde\varphi(z)=\lim_n\varphi(z_n)$ for any sequence $z_n\in D(T)$ with
$z_n\to z$ in $H$; the limit exists because $\varphi$ is bounded on a dense
subspace and $H$ is complete, and it does not depend on the sequence because a
bounded functional is uniformly continuous.

A vector $y\in H$ belongs to the **adjoint domain** $D(T^*)$ when the linear
functional $\varphi_y:D(T)\to\mathbb C$, $\varphi_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle$, is
bounded on $(D(T),\|\cdot\|)$. In that case Hilbert space Riesz representation
([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) applied to the extension
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$ produces a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with
$$T^*y\text{ is the unique }w\in H\text{ such that }\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,w\rangle\quad\text{for all }x\in D(T),$$
equivalently $\widetilde{\varphi_y}(z)=\langle z,T^*y\rangle$ for all $z\in H$.
The map $T^*:D(T^*)\to H$, $y\mapsto T^*y$, is the **adjoint** of $T$.

**Well-definedness.** The functional $\varphi_y$ is linear in $x$ for each
$y$, so its domain of boundedness $D(T^*)$ is a linear subspace: if
$\varphi_y,\varphi_{y'}$ are bounded so is $\varphi_{ay+by'}$ for scalars
$a,b$, because the first-variable-linear convention gives
$\varphi_{ay+by'}=\overline a\,\varphi_y+\overline b\,\varphi_{y'}$. On
$D(T^*)$ the map $T^*$ is linear: if $y,y'$ are represented by $w,w'$, then
$ay+by'$ is represented by $aw+bw'$, since
$\langle x,aw+bw'\rangle=\overline a\langle x,w\rangle+
\overline b\langle x,w'\rangle$; the representing vector is unique. By Riesz representation for the Hilbert space
$H$ a vector $w\in H$ is determined by the values $\langle z,w\rangle$ with
$z$ ranging over $H$, and those values are determined by the functional
$\widetilde{\varphi_y}$. Equivalently, if $w,w'$ both represent $\varphi_y$,
then $\langle x,w-w'\rangle=0$ for every $x\in D(T)$; density of $D(T)$ and
continuity of the inner product extend this equality to every $x\in H$, and
taking $x=w-w'$ gives $w=w'$. Finally only
ambient-norm boundedness of $\varphi_y$ on $D(T)$ is required: no extension,
no closure and no closedness of $T$ is presupposed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a densely defined linear operator on $H$.

- $T$ is **symmetric** when $T\subseteq T^*$, that is, $D(T)\subseteq D(T^*)$ and
  $Tx=T^*x$ for all $x\in D(T)$; equivalently
  $\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle$ for all $x,y\in D(T)$.
- $T$ is **self-adjoint** when $T=T^*$, that is, the domains and the values
  agree.
- $T$ is **essentially self-adjoint** when its closure $\overline T$ is
  self-adjoint; by [[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]] this presupposes
  that $T$ is closable.

**Consequences, with proofs.** These are part of the content of the definition.

1. *A symmetric $T$ is closable.* $T\subseteq T^*$ and $T^*$ is closed
   ([[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]]), so $T^*$ is a closed
   extension of $T$. In particular the closure $\overline T$ exists and
   $\overline T\subseteq T^*$.
2. *The closure of a symmetric operator is symmetric.* If $T\subseteq T^*$,
   the inclusion reversal of
   [[lem-unbounded-adjoint-is-well-defined-and-closed]] applied to
   $T\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq T^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$. Applying it once more to the inclusion
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^*$ gives $(T^*)^*\subseteq(T^{**})^*$, that is
   $T^{**}\subseteq T^{***}$. Since $\overline T=T^{**}$ and
   $(\overline T)^*=T^{***}$
   ([[thm-closable-iff-adjoint-domain-is-dense]]), this reads
   $\overline T\subseteq(\overline T)^*$: the closure is symmetric. (Each
   application is legitimate because the adjoint is defined once its operator
   is densely defined, and $D(T^{**})$ is dense because
   $T\subseteq T^{**}=\overline T$, so that $D(T^{**})$ contains the dense
   domain $D(T)$.)
3. *A self-adjoint operator has no proper symmetric extension.* If $T=T^*$ and
   $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*$, then $S^*\subseteq T^*$ by inclusion reversal,
   so $T\subseteq S\subseteq S^*\subseteq T^*=T$ and all inclusions are
   equalities.
4. *A self-adjoint operator is closed*, being equal to the adjoint $T^*$ of the
   densely defined $T$, and *an essentially self-adjoint operator has exactly
   one self-adjoint extension*, namely $\overline T$: a self-adjoint extension
   $S$ of $T$ is closed, hence contains the least closed extension
   $\overline T$, and then $S\subseteq S^*\subseteq(\overline T)^*=\overline T$
   by item 2 and symmetry, so $S=\overline T$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and $T$ a linear operator on $H$ with domain $D(T)$. Write $(z-T)x=zx-Tx$ for $x\in D(T)$. The **resolvent set**
of $T$ is
$$\rho(T):=\{z\in\mathbb C:\ z-T:D(T)\to H\text{ is bijective and }(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)\},$$
where $\mathcal B(H)$ is the space of bounded everywhere defined operators on
$H$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]); the **spectrum** is
$\sigma(T):=\mathbb C\setminus\rho(T)$. For $z\in\rho(T)$ the bounded operator
$$R_T(z):=(z-T)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)$$
is the **resolvent** of $T$ at $z$. This is the library convention used
throughout the page, matching the bounded resolvent of
[[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-of-a-bounded-operator]]: the shift is $zI-T$, with coefficient $-1$ on $T$.

**The resolvent determines $T$ back.** If $z\in\rho(T)$ and $R:=R_T(z)$, then
$D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $TRy=zRy-y$ for $y\in H$; equivalently
$T=zI-R^{-1}$ with $D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$, and $R(z-T)x=x$ for
$x\in D(T)$, $(z-T)Ry=y$ for $y\in H$.

**Nonempty resolvent set forces closedness, without the closed graph
theorem.** Assume $\rho(T)\ne\varnothing$ and fix $z\in\rho(T)$ with
$R:=R_T(z)$. Choose a bound $C\ge0$ such that $\|Rv\|\le C\|v\|$.
The map $F(v,w)=w-Rv$ is continuous, since
$\|F(v,w)-F(v',w')\|\le\|w-w'\|+C\|v-v'\|$.
Its zero set $\Gamma(R)=F^{-1}(\{0\})$ is closed. Because
$D(T)=\operatorname{ran}R$ and $(z-T)Rv=v$ for every $v\in H$, the graph of $T$ is
$$\Gamma(T)=\{(x,Tx):x\in D(T)\}=\{(Rv,zRv-v):v\in H\}=\Phi(\Gamma(R)),$$
where $\Phi(v,w):=(w,zw-v)$ is a continuous linear bijection of $H\oplus H$ with
continuous inverse $\Psi(u,v)=(zu-v,u)$, since $\Phi(\Psi(u,v))=(u,z u-(zu-v))=(u,v)$
and $\Psi(\Phi(v,w))=\Psi(w,zw-v)=(v,w)$. A homeomorphism carries closed sets
to closed sets, so $\Gamma(T)$ is closed and $T$ is closed.
No closed graph theorem and hence no choice principle is used here.

For the zero operator on a nonzero $H$, $\rho(0)=\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$: the nonzero shifts have inverse $z^{-1}I$, whereas the zero shift is not bijective. If $H=\{0\}$, every shift is the unique bijection of the zero space, so $\rho(T)=\mathbb C$ and $\sigma(T)=\varnothing$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$.

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or
complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let $T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a
compact self-adjoint operator ([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]]). Then $T$ has a
Hilbert basis ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]])
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]): one may take the union
of orthonormal bases of the finitely many-dimensional nonzero eigenspaces with a
Hilbert basis of $\ker T$. If $\ker T=\{0\}$ no vectors from the kernel are
needed, and if all nonzero eigenspaces are absent (that is $T=0$) the union is a
Hilbert basis of $H=\ker T$.

Let $W$, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. If
$T:X\to Y$ is compact ([[def-compact-linear-operator]]) and $A:W\to X$ and
$B:Y\to Z$ are bounded linear operators ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), then
the composites $TA:W\to Y$ and $BT:X\to Z$ are compact.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$. Then every nonreal number belongs to
$\rho(T)$: $\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb R\subseteq\rho(T)$. More precisely, for
$z=a+ib$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $b\ne0$, and every $x\in D(T)$,
$$\|(T-z)x\|^2=\|(T-a)x\|^2+b^2\|x\|^2 ,$$
and consequently $\|R_T(z)\|\le 1/|\operatorname{Im}z|$. In particular
$\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb R$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]],
[[def-countable-choice]]). Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on an
infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space $H$
([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]],
[[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-dimension]]), let $c\in\mathbb R$ lie in the
resolvent set of $A$, and assume that the resolvent
$R_c:=(A-c)^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)$ is compact
([[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]],
[[def-compact-linear-operator]]). Then:

(a) $H$ has a complete orthonormal family $(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of
eigenvectors of $A$; writing $\mu_n$ for the eigenvalue of $e_n$, one has
$|\mu_n|\to\infty$ (each eigenvalue repeated according to its finite
multiplicity), and every eigenspace of $A$ is finite dimensional;

(b) $\sigma(A)$ consists exactly of the eigenvalues $\mu_n$ of $A$ and has no
other points, and the essential spectrum is empty:
$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)=\varnothing$
([[def-discrete-and-essential-spectrum-of-a-self-adjoint-operator]]); thus
every spectral point of $A$ is an isolated eigenvalue of finite
multiplicity;

(c) for every $z$ in the resolvent set of $A$ the resolvent $(A-z)^{-1}$ is
compact.

derivations.claim: [Symmetry] For $x,y\in D(A)=D(cA)$, [F2] gives $\langle(cA)x,y\rangle=c\langle Ax,y\rangle=c\langle x,Ay\rangle=\langle x,cAy\rangle=\langle x,(cA)y\rangle$; since $c$ is real, the scalar passes through the pairing in both slots, so $cA$ is symmetric.

[Resolvent identity] Fix $z\in\mathbb C$ and write $B:=cA-z$ and $B':=A-z/c$ on the common domain $D(A)$. Then $B=cB'$ as operators, since $c(A-z/c)x=cAx-zx=(cA-z)x$ for every $x\in D(A)$. If $z/c\in\rho(A)$, then $B'$ is a bijection $D(A)\to H$ with bounded inverse, so $B=cB'$ is a bijection with inverse $c^{-1}B'^{-1}\in\mathcal B(H)$, which is the displayed identity; conversely if $z\in\rho(cA)$, then $c^{-1}B=B'$ is a bijection with bounded inverse $c\,B^{-1}$, so $z/c\in\rho(A)$. Therefore $\rho(cA)=c\,\rho(A)$ and, taking complements in $\mathbb C$, $\sigma(cA)=c\,\sigma(A)$; this is (b).

[Eigenpairs] Let $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and $x\in H$, $x\ne0$. Since $D(cA)=D(A)$, $x\in D(A)$ if and only if $x\in D(cA)$. For such $x$, $Ax=\lambda x$ if and only if $cAx=c\lambda x$, because multiplication by $c\ne0$ is injective; hence the eigenspaces coincide, which is (d).

[Adjoint domain] Let $y\in D((cA)^*)$. Then $x\mapsto\langle(cA)x,y\rangle=c\langle Ax,y\rangle$ is bounded on $D(A)$, and since $c>0$, $x\mapsto\langle Ax,y\rangle$ is bounded on $D(A)$ as well; hence $y\in D(A^*)=D(A)$ and $A^*y=Ay$. For every $x\in D(A)$ the defining identity of the adjoint and [F2] then give $\langle x,(cA)^*y\rangle=\langle(cA)x,y\rangle=c\langle Ax,y\rangle=c\langle x,Ay\rangle=\langle x,cAy\rangle$, and density of $D(A)$ in $H$ gives $(cA)^*y=cAy$. Hence $D((cA)^*)\subseteq D(cA)$; the reverse inclusion holds because $cA$ is symmetric, so $D((cA)^*)=D(cA)$ and $(cA)^*=cA$. This proves (a).

[All resolvents are compact] Write $R_z=(A-z)^{-1}$ and suppose $R_{z_0}$ is compact. The resolvent identity, obtained by subtracting the two inverses on their common operator domain, is $R_z=R_{z_0}+(z-z_0)R_{z_0}R_z=R_{z_0}[I+(z-z_0)R_z]$. Thus every $R_z$ is compact by [F5], irrespective of whether $z_0$ is real. Step 1.2 now gives compactness of every resolvent of $cA$.

[Finite-dimensional case] If $\dim H=N<\infty$, the dense linear domain $D(A)$ equals $H$, since every finite-dimensional subspace is closed ([[cor-finite-dimensional-subspaces-are-closed]]). The operator $A$ is then bounded and compact, and its self-adjointness and [F5] give an orthonormal eigenbasis of precisely $N$ vectors, including a basis of its zero eigenspace if necessary. In that basis $A$ is the diagonal matrix with real entries $\mu_j$, so its spectrum is exactly those entries: off that set the diagonal inverse exists and is bounded, while at an entry there is a nonzero kernel vector. Step 1.3 gives the same family for $cA$, and step 1.2 gives the scaled spectrum.

[Infinite-dimensional eigenfamily from an arbitrary compact resolvent] Suppose $H$ is infinite dimensional. By step 2.2 both $R_i$ and $R_{-i}$ are compact; their adjoint relation $R_i^*=R_{-i}$ follows from the defining self-adjoint pairings, and the resolvent identity shows they commute. Hence $K:=R_{-i}R_i=R_i^*R_i$ is compact, self-adjoint, positive and injective. Its range lies in $D(A^2)$: $R_i$ maps into $D(A)$, $R_{-i}$ preserves $D(A)$ and commutes there with $A$, by $(A-z)R_z=I$ and $R_z(A-z)=I$ on $D(A)$. [F5] decomposes $H$ into the closed span of its finite-dimensional positive $K$-eigenspaces $E_
u$, with no kernel part. For $e\in E_
u$, $e=
u^{-1}Ke\in D(A^2)$ and $K(Ae)=A(Ke)=
u Ae$, so $E_
u$ is invariant under $A$. The restriction of $A$ there is a finite-dimensional self-adjoint operator; step 2.3 gives an orthonormal eigenbasis of that restriction. The union is a complete orthonormal eigenfamily of $A$. If $Ae=\mu e$, direct resolvent evaluation gives $Ke=(\mu^2+1)^{-1}e$. There are only finitely many such vectors with $|\mu|\le M$ for each fixed $M$, since [F5] gives only finitely many $K$-eigenvalues above $(M^2+1)^{-1}$ and each has finite multiplicity. The union is countable and infinite, hence can be indexed by $\mathbb N$ under the retained choice assumptions, and $|\mu_n|	o\infty$.

[No additional spectrum] In the eigenbasis of step 3.1, self-adjointness gives $\langle Ax,e_n\rangle=\mu_n\langle x,e_n\rangle$ for $x\in D(A)$, so $\sum_n\mu_n^2|\langle x,e_n\rangle|^2=\|Ax\|^2$. Conversely, if this sum is finite, the finite sums $x_N$ and $Ax_N$ converge to $x$ and $y:=\sum_n\mu_n\langle x,e_n\rangle e_n$; passing to the limit in $\langle Ax_N,v\rangle=\langle x_N,Av\rangle$ for every $v\in D(A)$ puts $x$ in $D(A^*)=D(A)$ and gives $Ax=y$. Thus $A$ has exactly this maximal diagonal domain. Since $|\mu_n|\to\infty$, a complex $z$ outside $\{\mu_n\}$ has positive distance from that set. The diagonal map with entries $(\mu_n-z)^{-1}$ is bounded and maps $H$ into the displayed domain because $\sup_n|\mu_n/(\mu_n-z)|<\infty$; it is the two-sided inverse of $A-z$. Every $\mu_n$ is an eigenvalue. This proves $\sigma(A)=\{\mu_n\}$, and steps 1.2 and 1.3 give the scaled spectrum and common eigenfamily, completing (c).

[Quadratic forms] If $\langle Ax,x\rangle\ge\gamma\|x\|^2$ for every $x\in D(A)$, then for $x\in D(cA)=D(A)$ the same inequality scaled by $c>0$ gives $\langle(cA)x,x\rangle=c\langle Ax,x\rangle\ge c\gamma\|x\|^2$; this is (e), and steps 2.1, 1.2, 2.3, 4.1 and 1.3 complete the proof.

boundaries.evidence: The Hilbert space is nonzero and $D(A)$ is dense by hypothesis; step 1.2 treats every complex $z$ and no empty index set arises.

Step 1.3 excludes the zero vector from the eigenvector statement and step 3.1 scales the form inequality by $c>0$; the zero operator values are carried through steps 1.1 and 1.2 without division by $c$ beyond the nonzero factor $c$.
Step 1.3 treats a single eigenvector and step 1.2 a single resolvent, so the one-dimensional and one-eigenvector cases are included.
Step 1.3 proves the equivalence $Ax=\lambda x$ iff $cAx=c\lambda x$ for every eigenvector, with no simplicity or multiplicity assumption.
Step 1.2 treats the resolvent set as the complement of the spectrum and makes no boundary assertion about it; step 3.1 states the form inequality on the whole domain $D(A)$.
The compact-resolvent clause of step 2.2 inherits the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice from the cited eigenbasis lemma, and steps 1.1, 1.3 and 3.1 select nothing.
Step 1.2 proves the forward implication: if $z/c$ lies in the resolvent set of $A$, then $z$ lies in the resolvent set of $cA$ with the displayed inverse.
Step 1.2 proves the reverse implication: if $z$ lies in the resolvent set of $cA$, then $c^{-1}B=B'$ is a bijection with bounded inverse and $z/c$ lies in the resolvent set of $A$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $m,\hbar>0$, put
$c:=2\pi^2\hbar^2/m$, and let $H_0$ be the free one-dimensional operator of
[[thm-nrqm-composites-real-multipliers-and-free-bounded-potential-operators]]
clause (b) with $d=1$, this $c$ and $b=0$:
$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^{*}M_{c|\xi|^2}\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\bigl\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb C):|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in L^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)\bigr\},$$
where $\mathcal F_2$ is the unitary Plancherel transform of that theorem and
$M_{c|\xi|^2}$ is multiplication by the function $\xi\mapsto c|\xi|^2$. Let
$D^2$ denote the second weak derivative, defined componentwise on the
locally integrable classes of $\mathbb R$
([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]), and let
$W^{2,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ be the Sobolev space
([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]). Then:

(a) $D(H_0)=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ as sets and
$$H_0f=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\,D^2f\qquad\text{for every }f\in D(H_0);$$
equivalently, $\mathcal F_2(H_0f)(\xi)=c|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f(\xi)$ and
$\mathcal F_2\bigl(-\tfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}D^2f\bigr)(\xi)=c|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f(\xi)$
for almost every $\xi$, and the two $L^2$ classes agree.

(b) For every real bounded measurable $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, the operator
$H_0+M_V$ of clause (c) of the cited theorem, with domain $D(H_0)$, coincides
with the operator $f\mapsto-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}D^2f+Vf$ on the same domain; in
particular, for $E\in\mathbb R$ and $\psi\in W^{2,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$ the
eigenvalue equation $(H_0+M_V)\psi=E\psi$ is equivalent to the weak equation
$-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}D^2\psi+V\psi=E\psi$ elementwise in $L^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$.

The statement identifies operators on the same domain; it asserts neither
smoothness of the classes in $W^{2,2}$ nor any physical interpretation.

**(a) Assigned sharp observables.** Adopt the observable and probability postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-observable-and-probability]] (P2) for a declared system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned sharp observable** of the system is a pair $(A,u_A)$ consisting of a densely defined self-adjoint operator $A:D(A)\subset H\to H$ on the assigned Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]) and a **declared unit** $u_A$ in which the real spectral coordinate of $A$ is read, in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. The domain $D(A)$ is part of the assignment: symmetry on a smaller domain, or a formal differential expression, does not by itself supply an assigned observable ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]). Whether a concrete laboratory quantity of a given apparatus is described by a particular pair $(A,u_A)$ is a tested identification with uncertainty under the preparation and apparatus postulate P7 and is not produced by this definition.

**(b) Spectral measure and outcome law.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), the choice hypotheses of the cited spectral suppliers. The self-adjoint operator $A$ has a unique spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$, with $D(A)=\{x:\int\lambda^{2}\,dE_{A,x}<\infty\}$ and $Ax=\int\lambda\,dE_A(\lambda)x$, where $E_{A,x}(B)=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]). For a preparation $\rho$, that is a state $\rho\in D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], the **outcome law** of the pair $(A,u_A)$ in the preparation $\rho$ is the assignment
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_A(B)\bigr)\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P2; for the pure preparation $[\psi]$ of a unit vector $\psi$ it is $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_A(B)\psi\|^{2}$, which depends only on the ray by [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. The law is a probability measure on the Borel sets by [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b), and it is affine in the preparation: for a statistical mixture $\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ one has $\mu^{A}_{\sum_nw_n\rho_n}=\sum_nw_n\mu^{A}_{\rho_n}$ by [[lem-nrqm-observables-outcome-law-affinity-and-trace-norm-continuity]] clause (b).

**(c) Outcome sets and exact values.** A declared finite-resolution outcome of the quantity is a Borel set $B$; its probability in the preparation $\rho$ is $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$, and a "value in $B$" is read only through this number. The reading of an **exact value** $\lambda$ is the singleton $B=\{\lambda\}$, with probability $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})$; by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-measure-atoms-and-eigenvalues]] clauses (a) and (b) this number is zero for every preparation unless $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, and when $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue it is the total weight of the eigenspace. In particular the model provides no normalizable eigenvector at a non-eigenvalue of $A$. If $A$ has no eigenvalues, every preparation has an atomless outcome law: each singleton has probability zero, while $\mathbb R$ remains the outcome space and the law is concentrated on $\sigma(A)$ as in clause (d). Zero singleton probability does not exclude real point values as realizations of this law; it supplies no normalized exact-value eigenstate. A finite-resolution record is read through its declared Borel bin, in the sense of clause (iii) of P2.

**(d) Spectral support.** The outcomes of the observable lie in its spectrum: with $\sigma(A)$ the spectrum of [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]], one has $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B\cap\sigma(A))$ and $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\sigma(A))=1$ for every preparation by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-support-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). This is the precise reading of the statement that the result of a measurement lies in the spectrum of the observable.

**(e) Moments.** The **mean** and the **variance** of the outcome law in a preparation are the numbers $\int\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ and $\int(\lambda-m)^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ with $m$ the mean, read in the declared unit $u_A$ and its square respectively; they exist only under the integrability hypotheses of [[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]], which also supplies the formulas in terms of $A$ and the state. For a pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi\in D(A)$ the mean and the second moment are $\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$ and $\|A\psi\|^{2}$; membership of $\psi$ in $D(A)$ or in $D(A^{2})$ is a genuine hypothesis and is not asserted for an arbitrary preparation.

**(f) Unsharp finite outcomes are separate.** Clause (iv) of P2 permits a finite family of bounded effects $F_a$ with $0\le F_a\le I$ and $\sum_aF_a=I$ and outcome probabilities $\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$ as an operational description of a finite-resolution apparatus. That extension is tied to an apparatus instrument and is developed, together with state updates, on the measurement-and-instruments page; this definition fixes only the sharp outcome law of clause (b) and makes no claim that every laboratory procedure realizes it.

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the spectral theorem, assert no dynamics, no joint measurement of several observables, no detector realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any physical system is exactly described by an assigned pair $(A,u_A)$. The additive additivity, support, atom and moment statements cited are mathematical consequences proved in the cited items; their physical reading is exactly the reading of P2 fixed here.

**(a) Assigned energy observable.** Adopt the autonomous-dynamics postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]] (P4) for a declared isolated system whose state space is the model's [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]. An **assigned energy observable** of the system is an assigned sharp observable $(H_{\mathrm{op}},u_H)$ in the sense of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (a), whose declared unit $u_H$ is an energy unit in the sense of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]] (joules in the SI conventions fixed there). Thus $H_{\mathrm{op}}:D(H_{\mathrm{op}})\subset H\to H$ is densely defined and self-adjoint ([[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]], [[def-hilbert-space]]), with spectral projection-valued measure $E_H$ on the Borel sets of $\mathbb R$ under the choice hypotheses of [[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]] ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and its outcome law in a preparation is the law of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). The assignment of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ is part of the model specification, as in clause (i) of P4; this definition asserts nothing about which laboratory quantity of a concrete system realizes it.

**(b) The unitary flow.** The **time evolution** or **flow** of the isolated system is the family
$$U(t):=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{i}{\hbar}tH_{\mathrm{op}}\Bigr):=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\,dE_H(\lambda)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P4 in the spectral calculus of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ ([[def-unbounded-integral-against-a-pvm]]); here $\hbar>0$ is the reduced Planck constant with its value and unit fixed by [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]], so that $tH_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ is dimensionless. Equivalently, $U(t)=e^{itT}$ for the self-adjoint generator $T:=-H_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar$ with $D(T)=D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$; the two readings agree by the uniqueness of the generator in Stone's theorem, and by [[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]] ([[lem-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-flow-calculus]] clause (a)) the family $U$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group: $U(0)=I$, $U(t+s)=U(t)U(s)$, $U(t)^{*}=U(t)^{-1}=U(-t)$ ([[def-strongly-continuous-one-parameter-unitary-group]]).

**(c) Schroedinger picture.** The **Schroedinger-picture evolution** of a preparation is fixed by clause (iii) of P4. A state vector evolves by $\psi(t):=U(t)\psi(0)$ for every $\psi(0)\in H$, and the **state at time $t$** of the pure preparation $[\psi(0)]$ is the pure preparation $[\psi(t)]$, which is well defined because $U(t)$ is injective; a general preparation $\rho$, that is an element of the state space $D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]], evolves by
$$\rho(t):=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*},$$
the reading of clause (iii) of P4 in the density-operator vocabulary of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]] ([[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]). In this picture the assigned observables are held fixed at their assigned values and the preparation moves.

**(d) Heisenberg picture.** For a **bounded** assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ — that is, an assigned sharp observable with $A\in\mathcal B(H)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]), so that $A$ is self-adjoint and everywhere defined — the **Heisenberg representative** of $(A,u_A)$ at time $t$ is the pair $(A_H(t),u_A)$ with the same declared unit and
$$A_H(t):=U(t)^{*}AU(t)=U(-t)AU(t).$$
By [[lem-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-heisenberg-flow]] clauses (a) and (d), $A_H(t)$ is again bounded and self-adjoint with spectral projection-valued measure $E_{A_H(t)}(B)=U(-t)E_A(B)U(t)$, so $(A_H(t),u_A)$ is again an assigned sharp observable of the framework; in this picture the preparation is held fixed at its value at time $0$ and the observables move. The two pictures are two bookkeeping devices for the same model; the statement that they assign the same outcome laws is proved in the Heisenberg-picture theorem of this page, not assumed here.

**(e) Stationary preparations.** A preparation $\rho\in D(H)$ is **stationary** for the assigned energy observable when $\rho(t)=\rho$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$. A pure preparation $[\psi]$ is stationary when $[\psi(t)]=[\psi(0)]$ for every $t$, that is, when the evolved vector remains in the ray of $\psi$; the characterization of this condition by the eigenrays of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ is proved in the stationary-states theorem of this page, not assumed here. An **energy eigenstate** is a pure preparation of a unit eigenvector of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$, and a **stationary state** in the model is a stationary pure preparation; by that theorem the two notions coincide.

**(f) Energy-compatible observables.** An assigned sharp observable $(A,u_A)$ is **compatible with the energy**, or **energy-compatible**, when its spectral projection-valued measure and that of the energy commute strongly,
$$E_A(B)E_H(C)=E_H(C)E_A(B)\qquad\text{for all Borel }B,C\subseteq\mathbb R .$$
This is an equality of bounded operators on $H$, not a relation between formal commutators on a small domain; the phrase **conserved quantity** for an energy-compatible assigned observable is a claim about the time invariance of its outcome law and is established in the energy-conservation theorem of this page for bounded $A$.

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P4 together with P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P4, P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the cited mathematics, assert no dynamics for a prescribed time-dependent family or for an open system (clauses (iv) and (v) of P4 are separate model assumptions treated on their own pages), assert no measurement model, no apparatus realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any laboratory system is exactly isolated.

Adopt the state and composition postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-state-and-composition]] (P1), the observable and probability postulate in the reading of [[def-nrqm-observables-framework-observable-and-outcome-law]] (P2), and the autonomous-dynamics postulate [[post-nrqm-framework-autonomous-dynamics]] (P4), and assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $(H_{\mathrm{op}},u_H)$ be the assigned energy observable of a declared isolated system with state space $H$ ([[def-nrqm-state-geometry-framework-state-space]]), spectral projection-valued measure $E_H$ and flow $U(t)=\exp(-itH_{\mathrm{op}}/\hbar)$ ([[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]]), and write $\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*}$. Then:

(a) **Energy law and moments.** For every preparation $\rho$, every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ and every $t$,
$$\mu^{H_{\mathrm{op}}}_{\rho(t)}(B)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho(t)E_H(B)\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho(0)E_H(B)\bigr)=\mu^{H_{\mathrm{op}}}_{\rho(0)}(B);$$
for the pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi$ likewise $\|E_H(B)U(t)\psi\|^{2}=\|E_H(B)\psi\|^{2}$. If $\psi(0)\ne0$ and $\psi(0)\in D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$, the mean and second moment of the energy law of the pure preparation $[\psi(0)]$ are finite and time-independent. For any nonzero representative $\psi(0)$ their time-zero values are
$$\frac{\langle H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi(0),\psi(0)\rangle}{\|\psi(0)\|^{2}}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{\|H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi(0)\|^{2}}{\|\psi(0)\|^{2}},$$
respectively. The displayed conservation of moments makes no assertion that these moments are finite for preparations outside this domain hypothesis.

(b) **Conserved sharp observables.** Let $(A,u_A)$ be a bounded assigned sharp observable that is compatible with the energy ([[def-nrqm-autonomous-dynamics-framework-evolution]] clause (f)). Then its outcome law is time-independent: for every preparation $\rho$, every Borel set $B$ and every $t$,
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho(t)}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho(0)}(B).$$

(c) **Stationary states are exactly the eigenrays.** Let $\psi\in H$, $\psi\ne0$. The pure preparation $[\psi]$ is stationary, that is $[\psi(t)]=[\psi(0)]$ for every $t$, if and only if $\psi$ is an eigenvector of $H_{\mathrm{op}}$: $\psi\in D(H_{\mathrm{op}})$ and $H_{\mathrm{op}}\psi=\lambda\psi$ for some $\lambda\in\mathbb R$. In that case $\psi(t)=e^{-it\lambda/\hbar}\psi(0)$ for every $t$, and every assigned sharp observable has a time-independent outcome law in this preparation: $\mu^{A}_{[\psi(t)]}(B)=\mu^{A}_{[\psi(0)]}(B)$ for every $(A,u_A)$, every Borel $B$ and every $t$.

(d) **Status and exclusions.** No equilibration, relaxation, decay or convergence of the law of an arbitrary preparation is asserted; no moment beyond those finite at time zero is claimed; the converse of (b) — constancy of the law of a bounded observable in every preparation implying strong spectral compatibility with the energy — is not asserted for a general (possibly unbounded) $H_{\mathrm{op}}$; and the item is conditional on the isolated-system idealization of P4, asserting no apparatus realization and no empirical result.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]), let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on $H$ with spectral projection-valued measure $E_A$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]], [[def-projection-valued-measure]]), and let $E_{A,x}(B):=\langle E_A(B)x,x\rangle$ be its scalar measures ([[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]]). For $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ say that $\lambda$ is an **eigenvalue** of $A$ when $Ax=\lambda x$ for some nonzero $x\in D(A)$, the domain-restricted reading of [[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]. Then:

(a) The orthogonal projection $E_A(\{\lambda\})$ is the projection of $H$ onto the eigenspace $\ker(A-\lambda)=\{x\in D(A):Ax=\lambda x\}$; in particular $E_A(\{\lambda\})\ne0$ if and only if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.

(b) For every density operator $\rho$ on $H$, that is every self-adjoint positive trace-class $\rho$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)), the number $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(\{\lambda\}))$ is the weight that the scalar law $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ assigns to the singleton $\{\lambda\}$: it vanishes for every $\rho$ whenever $\lambda$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$, and it equals $1$ for the pure state $T_{u,u}$ of every unit eigenvector $u\in\ker(A-\lambda)$.

(c) If $A$ has no eigenvalues at all, then $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})=0$ for every density operator $\rho$ and every $\lambda\in\mathbb R$: the scalar law of every state carries no point mass, while its values on general Borel sets remain $\operatorname{tr}(\rho E_{A}(B))$.

Clauses (a)-(c) are mathematical statements about $A$, $E_A$ and the density operators; no physical interpretation of $\mu^{A}_{\rho}$ is asserted here.

derivations.claim: [The energy operator is an assigned observable] The operator $H_{V}=H_{0}^{\mathrm{lin}}+M_{V}$ is exactly the operator of [F1] for the bounded measurable $V$, so it is self-adjoint on $D(H_{V})=W^{2,2}(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, bounded below by $-\|V\|_{\infty}$, and densely defined; [F2] identifies its action as $-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}D^{2}+V$. The declared energy unit joule is a unit for the real spectral coordinate of $H_{V}$ under the conventions of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]], so the pair $(H_{V},\mathrm J)$ meets the definition [F3] of an assigned sharp observable; this is (a).

[Flow and Schroedinger equation] By clause (c) of the model, $H_{V}$ is adopted as the energy observable of the model's isolated system in the sense of clause (i) of P4; [F4] applied to the assigned energy observable $(H_{V},\mathrm J)$ therefore gives that $U(t)=\exp(-itH_{V}/\hbar)$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group, that the Schroedinger equation holds in the norm-differentiable sense exactly for initial vectors in $D(H_{V})$, and that $\rho(t)=U(t)\rho(0)U(t)^{*}$ is a density operator for every $t$; this is (b).

[Stationary rays and the energy atom] By [F5], $[\psi]$ is stationary if and only if $\psi$ is an eigenvector of $H_{V}$, and then $\psi(t)=e^{-itE/\hbar}\psi(0)$; the energy law is time-independent, and if $\psi(0)\in D(H_{V})$ the mean and second moment are finite and time-independent with values $\langle H_{V}\psi,\psi\rangle=E\|\psi\|^{2}=E$ and $\|H_{V}\psi\|^{2}=E^{2}\|\psi\|^{2}=E^{2}$ for a unit eigenvector. By [F6] the time-independent law of the unit eigenvector assigns probability one to $\{E\}$. Clauses (b) of [F5] give the conservation statement for bounded compatible observables, completing (c).

[Position reading] Clause (b) of the model declares the outcome law of the position assignment $Q$ in a unit class $\psi$ to be $\mu^{Q}_{\psi}(B)=\int_{B}|\psi|^{2}dx$; this reading is part of the model and is not derived here. For a unit eigenvector both readings are those of the same preparation through the two declared observables $(H_{V},\mathrm J)$ and $Q$, and no joint law, joint measurement or compatibility of $Q$ and $H_{V}$ is asserted; this is (d), and the exclusions of (e) are exactly those recorded in clause (f) of the model.

boundaries.evidence: The model state space is nonzero, $D(H_V)$ is dense by step 1.1, and the statements of a flow and of an eigenray use no empty family.
Step 1.1 includes the free case $V=0$ among the bounded measurable potentials, and step 4.1 excludes the zero vector from the preparations to which the position reading is applied.
The spin-zero line model is the stated one-component case; step 1.1 uses the scalar operator and step 3.1 a single eigenvector.
Step 3.1 treats eigenvalues through the eigenvalue equation and the atom lemma without assuming simplicity, so degenerate eigenvalues of $H_V$ are covered by the same stationary-ray criterion.
Step 2.1 gives the flow for all real times and the model is defined on the whole line; no boundary condition or endpoint datum enters.
The spectral assignments of step 1.1 and the flow of step 2.1 assume Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice as hypotheses of the cited spectral and dynamics suppliers, and nothing else is selected.
Step 3.1 proves the forward direction of the stationary criterion: a stationary ray is an eigenray, in the supplier's equivalence quoted there.
Step 3.1 also proves the reverse direction: an eigenvector of $H_V$ gives the stationary ray with the phase $e^{-itE/\hbar}$ quoted from the supplier.
